headline: Memories are not recordings—they're reconstructions that change each time we recall them
universal_truth: We don't remember what happened; we remember our last memory of what happened
fun_facts: Every time you recall a memory, you slightly alter it—memory is a game of telephone with yourself
Emotional intensity increases memory strength—that's why we vividly remember dramatic moments
Sleep is essential for memory consolidation—pulling all-nighters before exams backfires
discussion_questions: What childhood memory might you be misremembering?
How does knowing memories change affect how you view the past?
What moments from today do you want to remember years from now?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: You remember your first day of school, your wedding, that embarrassing moment. But here's the unsettling truth: those memories aren't recordings. They're reconstructions—rebuilt each time you recall them. And each rebuild changes them slightly.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: If memories change every time we access them, how can we trust them? Are our most cherished recollections accurate, or have they drifted into pleasant fictions over years of retelling?

options.text: Not entirely—they change with each recall and are influenced by present beliefs
options.response: Correct. Memory is more like a Wikipedia page than a photograph—it gets edited over time.

options.text: The core details remain accurate even if peripherals fade
options.response: Sometimes, but even core details can shift...

q1.title: Reconsolidation
q1.script: When you recall a memory, it becomes temporarily unstable—a state called reconsolidation. Your brain essentially re-saves it, incorporating your current state and context. This is why memories drift. Each recall is a subtle rewrite.

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Emotion Amplifies
q2.script: Emotionally intense moments trigger adrenaline and cortisol, which strengthen memory formation. That's why you remember where you were during major events. Your brain flags emotional moments as important—remember this.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Sleep To Remember
q3.script: During sleep, your hippocampus replays the day's events, transferring important memories to long-term storage. Without adequate sleep, this consolidation fails. All-nighters before exams actually hurt retention—sleep is studying.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Your memories are not objective history—they're stories you tell yourself about who you've been. Handle them gently. The past you remember is partly a creation of the present you.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 28—four weeks of learning! Tomorrow, we'll explore why time feels different in different moments. Until then, notice: which memories are you rebuilding most often?
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Memory Gardening - Choose Your Recalls
growTrack.learning_objective: Be intentional about which memories you revisit
growTrack.activity: Think of a positive memory and spend 2 minutes vividly recalling it—the details, the feelings, the people. Then do the same with a difficult memory you've been ruminating on. Notice: the first one you strengthen, the second you might choose to recall less.
